notes: Out-of-time boundary appeal; estoppel from 1931 conveyance allowed but fact findings refused.

enrichment.short_title: Herbert v Pegrum: boundary estoppel and late appeal on watercourse conveyance
key_facts: The dispute concerned the boundary between Posada and Gaumont House in Barnstaple, formerly separated by a stream later culverted.
The county court judge found the boundary on the southern bank of the stream by estoppel arising from a 1931 conveyance clause granting road rights over the watercourse.
Mr and Mrs Pegrum applied out of time for permission to appeal after their solicitor declined to appeal at trial.
The eastern boundary was fixed by reference to a leylandii hedge, parts of which were disputed after judgment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal out of time with appeal to follow on a county court boundary dispute.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted and appeal allowed on the estoppel point; permission refused on findings of fact; surveyors directed to agree the adjusted boundary line.
enrichment.ratio: Words in a conveyance granting rights over a ditch or watercourse on the south side of property are at best ambiguous and insufficiently clear to estop the grantor from the normal presumption that the stream was divided laterally; late appeals on minor fact findings may properly be refused even where a point of law succeeds.
legal_issues: Whether clause 2 of the 1931 conveyance created estoppel fixing the boundary on the southern bank
Whether permission to appeal out of time should be granted
Whether the judge's findings of fact on the stream and hedge location were open to challenge
Appropriate costs where the claimant succeeded on a lesser boundary claim than argued below
catchwords: permission to appeal out of time

confidence.notes: Separate dispositions on estoppel and fact findings are clearly reasoned with a defined remedial order.

notes: Landmark MHA section 58 ECHR challenge; Silber J dismisses academic third claim but proposes case management reforms.

enrichment.short_title: R (B) v Dr SS: compulsory psychiatric treatment, capacity and section 58 MHA
key_facts: A detained patient initially challenged compulsory medical treatment but the RMO later agreed not to treat without consent, leaving a challenge to the lawfulness of section 58(3)(b).
The claimant argued section 58, read with the HRA, permits overriding a capacitous refusal only to protect the public or prevent serious harm to health.
The claim was academic because no immediate treatment was proposed and the main claims were dismissed by consent.
The judgment also addressed delays in judicial review challenges to second opinion approved doctor certificates.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Expedited rolled-up permission and substantive judicial review of the Secretary of State concerning compulsory treatment under the Mental Health Act 1983.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted but the third claim dismissed as academic; current law held not to breach Articles 3, 8 or 14 merely because a capacitous patient refuses consent; postscript proposed fast case management for SOAD challenges.
enrichment.ratio: An academic human rights challenge to compulsory treatment powers may be refused where no immediate benefit flows to the claimant; section 58 treatment of a capacitous refusing patient is not incompatible with Articles 3 or 8 merely because capacity exists and consent is withheld, nor does Article 14 require identical override rules for patients and non-patients.
legal_issues: Whether an academic claim against section 58(3)(b) should be entertained
Compatibility of compulsory treatment of capacitous patients with Articles 3 and 8 ECHR
Whether section 58 unlawfully discriminates under Article 14
Case management of challenges to SOAD treatment certificates

confidence.notes: Final disposition on the surviving claim is explicit though much of the judgment addresses academicity and procedural reform.

notes: First SOA 2003 sexual assault appeal; court explains two-stage section 78(b) test and dismisses appeal.

enrichment.short_title: R v H: first appeal on Sexual Offences Act 2003 sexual assault

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: The appellant was convicted at Teesside Crown Court of sexual assault under section 3 after grabbing a woman's tracksuit bottoms at night following a crude proposition.
The touching of clothing was held to constitute touching for section 3 purposes.
The judge failed to apply the two distinct limbs of section 78(b) separately in summing up.
Identification and alibi evidence from prosecution witnesses supported the appellant but the jury rejected it.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction following leave granted on referral by the Registrar.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction held safe despite misdirection on section 78(b) and minor Turnbull identification shortcomings.
enrichment.ratio: Section 78(b) requires both that touching because of its nature may be sexual and that because of circumstances or purpose it is sexual; touching clothing can be touching under section 79(8); where only the second limb is in issue a two-question jury direction is appropriate.
legal_issues: Whether grabbing tracksuit bottoms amounted to touching another person
Construction of section 78(b) and its relationship to R v Court
Whether the judge should have stopped the case
Adequacy of section 35 and identification directions

confidence.notes: Statutory analysis and appellate reasoning on safety of conviction are detailed and authoritative.

notes: Hague Convention appeal; settled children and child's objection findings upheld; forum shopping rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Re H (Children): Hague return refused where children settled in England
key_facts: A mother wrongfully removed children from Australia to England in August 2003 after the father believed the family was reuniting.
The father issued Hague proceedings over one year later, shortly before a scheduled Children Act merits hearing.
Hedley J found Chloe aged 13 and Quentin aged 5 settled in England and that Chloe objected to return.
The family was split between jurisdictions with siblings remaining in Australia.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from Hedley J against refusal to order return under the 1980 Hague Convention.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; findings on wrongful removal, settlement under Article 12, Chloe's objection under Article 13 and discretionary refusal upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Settlement is a factual state viewed primarily through the child's eyes and is not necessarily defeated by pending litigation; a father who chose domestic welfare proceedings rather than immediate Convention relief cannot complain when children become settled or object; Article 13 objection need not be tested against every hypothetical counterfactual.
legal_issues: Whether the children were settled in their new environment under Article 12
Whether retention rather than removal started the Article 12 clock on 8 November 2003
Whether Chloe objected to return within Article 13
Exercise of discretion under Articles 12, 13 and 18 against return
linked_authorities: Re S (A Minor) (Custody: Habitual Residence) [1998] AC 750

confidence.notes: Appellate endorsement of comprehensive first instance findings is clear on all Convention issues.

notes: DRC asylum and Article 3 rape-risk case; court criticises adjudicator reasoning and remits human rights claim.

enrichment.short_title: B v SSHD: Article 3 remittal where vulnerable young woman faces rape risk in DRC
key_facts: B, a young Congolese woman, claimed asylum after prolonged sexual enslavement by a soldier and severe PTSD.
An adjudicator allowed appeal on refugee and human rights grounds but conflated mental health and rape risks in his reasoning.
The IAT allowed the Secretary of State's appeal largely by reviewing facts rather than identifying errors of law.
The adjudicator found B would lack family support and medical treatment if returned and faced real risk of rape if homeless.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal on a point of law from an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision reversing an adjudicator.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; refugee status decision remitted; human rights claim remitted to a fresh adjudicator because Article 3 reasoning was deficient.
enrichment.ratio: Risk of psychiatric deterioration and risk of rape engage different legal tests under the Refugee Convention and Article 3 and must not be amalgamated without analysis; an individualised rape-risk finding for a vulnerable homeless young woman is not plainly bad in law and requires proper Article 3 reasoning on remittal.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator erred in granting refugee status
Whether return would breach Article 3 through mental health deterioration after N v SSHD
Whether individualised risk of rape engaged Article 3
Proper scope of IAT jurisdiction under section 101
linked_authorities: N v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2005] UKHL 31
Sinanduku v Secretary of State [2002] UKIAT 05060

confidence.notes: Appellate conclusions on remittal and legal defects are explicit though Article 3 application to rape remains unresolved.

notes: Solicitor negligence on opposing section 25 notice; summary judgment refused on loss-of-chance and estoppel points.

enrichment.short_title: Talisman v Norton Rose: negligent Landlord and Tenant Act section 25 notice
key_facts: Talisman acquired Park Royal premises where the true tenant may have been Wyko rather than Lewis DMR.
Norton Rose negligently served a section 25 notice on Wyko opposing a new tenancy on ground (f) instead of an unopposing notice.
Wyko quit and received about £179,000 section 37 compensation set off against dilapidations.
Talisman claimed the opposing notice caused or failed to avoid statutory compensation liability.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery application for summary judgment or strike out of professional negligence claim against solicitors.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; real prospect that estoppel, loss of chance of proving Wyko as tenant, and loss of negotiating chance could establish substantial loss.
enrichment.ratio: Section 37 compensation may become payable once ground (f) is asserted and the tenant quits regardless of causal link to quitting; a negligent opposing section 25 notice may cause recoverable loss if an unopposing notice could have avoided compensation through estoppel or negotiation; section 42(2) does not necessarily bar estoppel based on course of dealing.
legal_issues: Whether Talisman suffered loss beyond nominal damages from the incorrect notice
Whether Wyko rather than Lewis was the tenant by estoppel
Loss of chance of negotiating away section 37 liability
Whether compensation would have been payable via Lewis notices in any event
index_terms: Lloyds Bank v City of London
linked_authorities: Lloyds Bank plc v City of London [1983] 1 Ch 192

confidence.notes: Interlocutory decision with clear reasoning though liability and quantum remain for trial.

notes: Equitable charge appeal; Murray v Guinness rejected; constructive trust under section 2(5) upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Kinane v Mackie-Conteh: section 2(5) constructive trust for home charge agreement
key_facts: Mr Kinane lent £50,000 to Almack for a rice trading venture expecting 100 per cent return within 120 days.
Mr Mackie-Conteh signed a letter offering the family home as security for £100,000 before the loan was advanced.
The judge held the security agreement unenforceable under section 2(1) but enforceable via section 53(1)(c), which the Court of Appeal rejected.
Kinane advanced funds only after receiving the signed security letter and a £15,000 cheque.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against declaration of equitable charge and order for sale; cross-appeal on constructive trust.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; cross-appeal allowed; security enforced via constructive trust/proprietary estoppel under section 2(5) despite invalid written contract.
enrichment.ratio: Section 53(1)(c) applies only to disposition of subsisting equitable interests, not creation of a new charge; where a landowner induces a lender to advance money by delivering a signed security agreement representing it is binding, section 2(5) may enforce a constructive trust overlapping proprietary estoppel despite section 2(1).
legal_issues: Whether the security agreement complied with section 2(1) of the 1989 Act
Applicability of section 53(1)(c) following Murray v Guinness
Whether a constructive trust arose under section 2(5)
Effect of Actionstrength on estoppel and invalid agreements
linked_authorities: Actionstrength Ltd v International Glass Engineering SpA [2003] 2 AC 541

confidence.notes: Detailed appellate analysis of formalities and constructive trust is clearly reasoned.

notes: Preferred supplier contract construction; Field J allows Rugby's summary judgment appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Rugby Group v ProForce: construction of preferred supplier status clause
key_facts: ProForce signed a 2001 agreement to supply cleaning staff and buy machinery from Rugby Cement for a minimum two-year term.
The agreement stated ProForce would hold preferred supplier status during the contract period.
ProForce purchased expensive Vac Press and sweeper equipment and supplied defined personnel for two years.
From November 2001 Rugby used other agencies for non-cleaning labour, which ProForce claimed breached preferred supplier status.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from refusal of Rugby's application to strike out or obtain summary judgment on ProForce's breach of contract claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; claim struck out and summary judgment for Rugby; preferred supplier status did not oblige Rugby to use ProForce for all site labour.
enrichment.ratio: Where parties performed a subject-to-contract agreement, an implied binding contract arose on its terms; preferred supplier status means inclusion on any preferred list for all personnel categories if Rugby operates such a system, not an obligation to contract exclusively with ProForce or supply all labour requirements.
legal_issues: Whether subject-to-contract wording prevented enforceability after performance
Meaning of preferred supplier status in the factual matrix
Whether pre-contract negotiations and entire agreement clause 9.2 excluded background statements
Whether implied terms were necessary for commercial efficacy
linked_authorities: Investors Compensation Scheme Ltd v West Bromwich Building Society [1998] 1 WLR 896

confidence.notes: Final construction and procedural disposition on summary judgment are clearly stated.

notes: Section 67 GAFTA jurisdiction challenge; Chinese capacity voided July contract; April substitution upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Continental v Shandong: GAFTA jurisdiction and Chinese company capacity
key_facts: CEL contracted to sell 300,000 mt soybean meal to GROUPCO under a July 1997 GAFTA contract governed by English law.
GROUPCO lacked MOFTEC foreign trade capacity under its articles and the July contract was void under Chinese law.
In April 1998 GROUPCO's name was deleted and affiliate FTC substituted so a letter of credit could be opened.
CEL challenged a GAFTA appeal award finding no jurisdiction over GROUPCO after substitution.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court section 67 application to set aside GAFTA appeal award on substantive jurisdiction.
enrichment.outcome: Challenge failed; tribunal correctly held no arbitration agreement between GROUPCO and CEL survived void July contract and April principal substitution.
enrichment.ratio: A Chinese company without foreign trade capacity under its articles cannot validly enter the underlying GAFTA sale contract or a severable arbitration clause with a foreign seller; under Chinese commission agency rules FTC could not bind GROUPCO as principal and the April agreement substituted FTC rather than acting as GROUPCO's agent.
legal_issues: Whether GROUPCO had legal capacity to enter the July contract
Effect of absence of MOFTEC licence on validity and illegality
Whether April amendments substituted FTC or created agency for GROUPCO
Whether arbitration agreement survived invalidity of main contract
linked_authorities: Fiona Trust & Holding Corp v Privalov [2007] UKHL 40
Harbour Assurance Co Ltd v Kansa General International Insurance Co Ltd [1993] QB 701

confidence.notes: Fact findings on substitution and detailed Chinese law analysis support the jurisdictional conclusion.

notes: POCA cash forfeiture appeal; Moses J holds lies in context may prove unlawful source on balance of probabilities.

enrichment.short_title: Muneka v Customs: cash forfeiture under Proceeds of Crime Act 2002
key_facts: Bujar Muneka was stopped at Heathrow with £22,760 cash en route to Albania and gave inconsistent explanations.
He claimed earnings as an electrician and carrying money for others, but changed his account before the district judge.
Customs evidence showed low living expenses and unexplained bank deposits inconsistent with lawful income.
The district judge rejected Muneka's explanations as lies and ordered forfeiture as recoverable property.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from a magistrates' court forfeiture decision under section 298.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; district judge entitled to infer on the balance of probabilities that cash was obtained through or intended for unlawful conduct from rejected lies and supporting evidence.
enrichment.ratio: Under POCA the civil standard applies; prosecution need not identify a specific offence if unlawful conduct in the UK is proved; lies about source and destination asked in a forfeiture context may support inference that suggested unlawful source or use is true when no other reasonable explanation exists.
legal_issues: Whether lies alone could establish recoverable property under section 298
Whether a specific criminal offence must be identified
Application of balance of probabilities standard under section 241(3)
Whether a reverse burden of proof arose
linked_authorities: Bassick and Osborne v Commissioners of Customs and Excise [1993] 161 JP 377
Nevin v Customs and Excise (unreported, 3 November 1995)

confidence.notes: Statutory framework and factual inference principles are clearly applied to uphold the magistrates' decision.
